\section{Feature Correlation Matrix}
\label{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}

This appendix documents inter-feature correlations and the PCA analysis referenced in \S\ref{sec:results-differential}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Pearson correlation matrix of the seven depth features ($N=27{,}529$).}
\label{tab:feature-corr}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrr}
\toprule
 & $\bar{H}$ & $\sigma_H$ & $H_{\min}$ & $H_{\max}$ & $\tau$ & TTR & Hapax \\
\midrule
$\bar{H}$ & \textemdash & 0.49 & 0.31 & 0.01 & 0.07 & \textbf{0.86} & \textbf{0.81} \\
$\sigma_H$ & 0.49 & \textemdash & $-$0.15 & 0.16 & 0.26 & 0.43 & 0.34 \\
$H_{\min}$ & 0.31 & $-$0.15 & \textemdash & $-$0.04 & 0.01 & 0.20 & 0.23 \\
$H_{\max}$ & 0.01 & 0.16 & $-$0.04 & \textemdash & $-$0.08 & $-$0.13 & $-$0.15 \\
$\tau$ & 0.07 & 0.26 & 0.01 & $-$0.08 & \textemdash & 0.13 & 0.14 \\
TTR & \textbf{0.86} & 0.43 & 0.20 & $-$0.13 & 0.13 & \textemdash & \textbf{0.97} \\
Hapax & \textbf{0.81} & 0.34 & 0.23 & $-$0.15 & 0.14 & \textbf{0.97} & \textemdash \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

TTR and hapax ratio are near-perfectly correlated ($r=0.97$), and both correlate strongly with mean entropy ($r=0.86$ and $0.81$).
These three drifting features form a tightly coupled cluster: PCA on the standardized drifting-feature subset shows that a single principal component explains 92.3\% of their joint variance, with near-uniform loadings (0.56--0.59). These three features thus share a single latent dimension.
Full 7-feature PCA yields PC1 (44.4\% variance) loading on the drifting triplet (0.53--0.55) and PC2 (18.3\% variance) capturing entropy distributional shape (entropy std vs.\ entropy min contrast).
In contrast, $H_{\max}$, $\tau$ (tail decay), and $H_{\min}$ show weak pairwise correlations with all other features ($|r| < 0.27$); these features capture independent aspects of the token-probability distribution.

% Appendix — Length Confound Analysis
% Data source: 8-generator LOGO corpus (37,058 samples)

Surface diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) mechanically depend on text length:
shorter texts yield higher type-token ratios by construction.
If generation depth systematically shortens text, observed depth trends could be length artifacts rather than genuine distributional shifts.
We investigate with three complementary analyses.

\paragraph{(a) Length--depth correlation.}
Spearman rank correlation between word count and generation depth is weak across all eight generators ($|\rho| < 0.14$); depth does not systematically shorten or lengthen text in our corpus.

\paragraph{(b) Length--feature correlations.}
While length--depth correlation is weak, individual features show moderate length dependence:
tail\_decay ($|\rho| = 0.38$), hapax\_ratio ($|\rho| = 0.30$), and TTR ($|\rho| = 0.29$).
Reference-model features show weaker length correlations (entropy\_mean $|\rho| = 0.09$, entropy\_std $|\rho| = 0.18$).
This motivates the length-matched evaluation below: if length mediates some depth--feature association, controlling for length will reduce classification performance.

\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), then retrain the binary XGBoost classifier under pooled LOGO (8-fold).
Length-matched binary F1\,=\,0.724, down from 0.770 on the unmatched set ($\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.046).
To distinguish this from a sample-size effect, we run a random-subsample control at equal $N$ without length matching: F1\,=\,0.767, which confirms that the 0.046 drop reflects genuine length deconfounding rather than reduced data.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Length accounts for approximately 6\% of discriminative performance ($\Delta$\,=\,0.046 out of 0.770).
The majority of the depth signal is length-independent: length-matched F1 (0.724) remains far above chance and significantly above all individual detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Surface features (TTR, hapax\_ratio) partially co-vary with length, but their depth-discriminative contribution persists after length control, consistent with generation-induced vocabulary compression operating independently of text truncation.

\label{app:seed-control}

To test for topic-level leakage from shared seeds across generators, we construct an independent-seed evaluation where Pythia-2.8B and OLMo-2-1B use completely disjoint Wikipedia seed pools (500 seeds each, zero overlap).
Each generator produces depth-0 through depth-4 chains on its own seed pool; features are extracted with the same Pythia-410M reference model.
We then train a 7-feature XGBoost classifier on one generator's data and test on the other, in both directions.

\small

\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\

OLMo-2-1B $\rightarrow$ Pythia-2.8B & 0.666 & [0.643, 0.689] \\
\midrule
Independent-seed average & 0.680 & --- \\
Shared-seed LOGO (reference) & 0.694 & [0.688, 0.700] \\

The classifier thus captures generative degradation patterns rather than seed-specific topic content.}
\label{tab:seed-control}

The small gap ($-$1.4\,pp) between independent-seed and shared-seed evaluation falls within bootstrap confidence intervals, and both directions individually exceed 0.66.
Combined with the seed-level demeaning control (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), these results provide converging evidence that depth classification is driven by distributional properties of recursive generation, not topic identity.

Embedding cosine similarity between consecutive depth steps increases monotonically: 0$\rightarrow$1 (0.622), 1$\rightarrow$2 (0.683), 2$\rightarrow$3 (0.801), 3$\rightarrow$4 (0.859).

Table~\ref{tab:transfer} reports the full 8$\times$8 transfer matrix and Figure~\ref{fig:transfer} visualizes it as a heatmap.
Note that these classifiers are trained with a binary objective, whereas the LOGO classifiers in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} are trained on a 3-class task and evaluated on the binary subtask; the two setups are therefore not directly comparable.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{l|cccccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Train $\backslash$ Test} & \textbf{Py-2.8B} & \textbf{Py-1B} & \textbf{Qw-0.6B} & \textbf{Qw-1.7B} & \textbf{Qw-8B} & \textbf{OLMo-1B} & \textbf{Ll-3B} & \textbf{Mi-7B} \\
\midrule
Py-2.8B  & \underline{0.985} & 0.873 & 0.823 & 0.833 & 0.741 & 0.829 & 0.815 & 0.712 \\
Py-1B    & 0.834 & \underline{0.987} & 0.828 & 0.821 & 0.704 & 0.778 & 0.764 & 0.620 \\
Qw-0.6B  & 0.786 & 0.846 & \underline{0.991} & 0.851 & 0.786 & 0.795 & 0.760 & 0.680 \\
Qw-1.7B  & 0.794 & 0.839 & 0.859 & \underline{0.989} & 0.790 & 0.817 & 0.798 & 0.717 \\
Qw-8B   & 0.811 & 0.836 & 0.853 & 0.855 & \underline{0.984} & 0.848 & 0.839 & 0.790 \\
OLMo-1B  & 0.811 & 0.827 & 0.837 & 0.852 & 0.803 & \underline{0.988} & 0.828 & 0.763 \\
Ll-3B    & 0.856 & 0.860 & 0.845 & 0.851 & 0.798 & 0.851 & \underline{0.987} & 0.787 \\
Mi-7B    & 0.834 & 0.837 & 0.837 & 0.845 & 0.817 & 0.849 & 0.851 & \underline{0.969} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Cross-generator binary F1 transfer matrix (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Each row trains on one generator; each column evaluates on another. Diagonal entries (\underline{underlined}) are within-generator. All 56 off-diagonal pairs exceed chance (0.5). Classifiers use the same 7-feature XGBoost configuration as LOGO but are trained with a binary objective.}
\label{tab:transfer}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Heatmap of the cross-generator binary F1 transfer matrix (Table~\ref{tab:transfer}). Same-family pairs (e.g., Pythia$\leftrightarrow$Pythia, Qwen$\leftrightarrow$Qwen) show slightly higher transfer; Mi-7B is the hardest transfer target (column minimum 0.62) yet remains well above chance.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

All 56 off-diagonal transfer pairs yield F1 above chance, with a mean of 0.810 (95\% bootstrap CI [0.796, 0.822]; one-sample $t=46.58$, $p < 10^{-10}$).
Transfer is strongest within families (e.g., Py-2.8B$\to$Py-1B: 0.87) and weakest for Py-1B$\to$Mi-7B (0.62), consistent with the scale and reference-affinity effects discussed in \S\ref{sec:results-differential}.
These results confirm that depth signatures generalize across architectures, parameter scales, and model families, providing evidence against generator identity as a primary confound.

1	Figure~\ref{fig:cross-temp} shows cross-temperature transfer results for the 6-generator LOGO pipeline.
2	We evaluate four train$\rightarrow$test temperature conditions using Qwen3-1.7B data regenerated at $t{=}1.0$ (remaining five generators retain $t{=}0.7$).\footnote{The $t{=}1.0$ data uses top-$p{=}0.95$ (vs.\ $p{=}0.9$ for other configurations); this difference may contribute to the observed degradation beyond the temperature effect alone.}
3	
4	\begin{figure}[H]
5	\centering
6	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_appendix_cross_temp.pdf}
7	\caption{Cross-temperature transfer evaluation (6-gen LOGO). (a) Overall F1 by train$\rightarrow$test temperature condition. Matched conditions (0.7$\rightarrow$0.7, 1.0$\rightarrow$1.0) outperform cross-temperature transfer, with 0.7$\rightarrow$1.0 showing the largest degradation ($-6.6$\,pp in 3-class F1). (b) Per-generator 3-class F1 heatmap: Qwen3-1.7B shows dramatic degradation under cross-temperature conditions (0.418) while other generators remain stable. The temperature mismatch disproportionately affects the generator whose data was regenerated.}
8	\label{fig:cross-temp}
9	\end{figure}
10	
11	Key observations from the cross-temperature analysis:
12	
13	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
14	\item \textbf{Matched-temperature robustness}: Both $t{=}0.7$ and $t{=}1.0$ matched conditions yield comparable performance (3-class F1: 0.789 vs.\ 0.726), with the gap attributable to weaker depth signal at high temperature rather than classifier degradation.
15	
16	\item \textbf{Asymmetric transfer}: Training at $t{=}1.0$ and testing at $t{=}0.7$ (F1\,=\,0.791) transfers well, but the reverse (0.7$\rightarrow$1.0, F1\,=\,0.723) degrades. This asymmetry reflects the information structure: features learned from high-variance (high-temperature) data generalize to low-variance settings, but not vice versa.
17	
18	\item \textbf{Generator-specific vulnerability}: Qwen3-1.7B, the only generator with temperature-mismatched test data, drops to F1\,=\,0.418 under cross-temperature conditions while all other generators maintain F1 $>$ 0.76. This confirms that depth features are calibrated to the specific decoding regime.
19	
20	\item \textbf{Binary transfer for the mismatched generator}: For Qwen3-1.7B (the only generator with actual temperature mismatch), binary F1 drops from 0.948 to 0.713 under 0.7$\rightarrow$1.0 transfer but recovers in the reverse direction (1.0$\rightarrow$0.7: 0.948), consistent with the asymmetric pattern in Item 2. The aggregate binary range (0.900--0.958) is inflated by five generators whose data is identical across conditions.
21	\end{enumerate}
22

1	\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}
2	
3	To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).
4	
5	\begin{table}[ht]
6	\centering
7	\small
8	\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
9	\label{tab:clustering}
10	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
11	\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
12	\toprule
13	$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
14	\midrule
15	2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
16	3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
17	4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
18	\bottomrule
19	\end{tabular}}
20	\end{table}
21	
22	The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
23	At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
24	The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
25	At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.
26	
27	\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
28	To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
29	The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.
30	
31	\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
32	To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
33	Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
34	No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.
35	
36	\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
37	\label{app:tost-sensitivity}
38	
39	Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.
40	
41	\begin{table}[ht]
42	\centering
43	\small
44	\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
45	\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
46	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
47	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
48	\toprule
49	\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
50	\midrule
51	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
52	 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
53	 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
54	\midrule
55	Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
56	\midrule
57	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
58	 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
59	 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
60	\bottomrule
61	\end{tabular}}
62	\end{table}
63	
64	The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
65	Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
66	Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.
67	
68	\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
69	To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
70	we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
71	resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
72	score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
73	Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
74	reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
75	The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
76	is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
77	peak value in the sweep.
78	Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.49$) yields a
79	4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
80	The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
81	confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
82	$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
83	threshold choice.
84	
85	\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
86	\label{app:epsilon-sweep}
87	
88	The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
89	Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.
90	
91	\begin{table}[ht]
92	\centering
93	\small
94	\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
95	\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
96	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
97	\begin{tabular}{llcc}
98	\toprule
99	\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
100	\midrule
101	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.17 & 1.17 \\
102	 & TTR & 0.88 & 0.88 \\
103	 & hapax ratio & 0.76 & 0.76 \\
104	\midrule
105	Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.55 & 0.55 \\
106	\midrule
107	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
108	 & tail decay & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
109	 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
110	\bottomrule
111	\end{tabular}}
112	\end{table}
113	
114	\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.76$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.08$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.55$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
115	The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.
116	
117	\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
118	\label{app:holdout-split}
119	
120	To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
121	We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
122	Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
123	Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).
124	
125	\begin{table}[ht]
126	\centering
127	\small
128	\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
129	\label{tab:holdout-split}
130	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
131	\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
132	\toprule
133	& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
134	\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
135	\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
136	\midrule
137	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\
138	 & TTR & 0.61 & 0.59 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.59 & 0.01 \\
139	 & hapax ratio & 0.62 & 0.60 & 0.02 & 0.62 & 0.61 & 0.01 \\
140	\midrule
141	Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
142	\midrule
143	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.39 & 0.36 & 0.03 & 0.38 & 0.37 & 0.01 \\
144	 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.05 & 0.05 & 0.00 & 0.04 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\

149	
150	Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
151	However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
152	Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.
153	
154	Selection and validation subsets produce identical partitions in both splits (Table~\ref{tab:holdout-split}; Figure~\ref{fig:holdout-scatter}).
155	The maximum $\Delta|\rho|$ between selection and validation is 0.05 (entropy std, Split~B), and the minimum gap between adjacent zones remains $>$0.15 in all subsets.
156	
157	\begin{figure}[H]
158	\centering
159	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_ddr_holdout_split.pdf}
160	\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
161	\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
162	\end{figure}

164	\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
165	\label{app:heteroscedasticity}
166	
167	Levene tests reject equal variance between gen-1 and gen-2+ for drifting features ($p < 10^{-10}$; variance ratios 1.86--2.21).
168	To verify that the DDR partition is robust to this heteroscedasticity, we supplement pooled Cohen's $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ (using the gen-1 standard deviation as denominator) and Cliff's $\delta$ (a non-parametric ordinal effect size; Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes}).
169	
170	\begin{table}[ht]
171	\centering
172	\small
173	\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
174	\label{tab:effect-sizes}
175	\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
176	\toprule
177	\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\
178	\midrule
179	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & ent.\ mean & 1.054 & 1.410 & 0.587 \\
180	 & TTR & 0.814 & 1.116 & 0.510 \\
181	 & hapax ratio & 0.735 & 0.936 & 0.528 \\
182	\midrule
183	Intermediate & ent.\ std & 0.457 & 0.605 & 0.295 \\
184	\midrule
185	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & tail decay & 0.087 & 0.099 & 0.072 \\
186	 & ent.\ max & 0.062 & 0.065 & 0.021 \\
187	 & ent.\ min & 0.016 & 0.015 & 0.354$^{\dagger}$ \\
188	\bottomrule
189	\end{tabular}
190	\end{table}
191	
192	\noindent Effect sizes in Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes} are computed on the binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); the main text (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reports 3-class pooled $d$ values (e.g., hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), which are slightly larger because the gen-0/gen-1 contrast contributes additional separation.
193	Glass's $\Delta$ amplifies drifting effects (1.41 vs.\ 1.05 for entropy mean) because gen-2+ variance exceeds gen-1 variance (ratio 2.08), making the pooled Cohen's $d$ conservative.
194	Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
195	The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.
196	Cliff's $\delta$ classifies all drifting features as ``large'' ($|\delta| > 0.474$) and entropy std as ``small'' ($|\delta|{=}0.295$), consistent with the parametric partition.
197	
198	\noindent $^{\dagger}$Entropy min's elevated Cliff's $\delta$ (0.354, ``medium'') reflects distributional shape asymmetry between gen-1 and gen-2+ that rank-based statistics detect but location measures do not (Cohen's $d{=}0.016$, Glass's $\Delta{=}0.015$).
199	This is consistent with its documented boundary status (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}): the gen-0/gen-1 transition produces rank-order shifts that persist into deeper generations without affecting the mean.

\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
\label{tab:clustering}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
\toprule
$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
\midrule
2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.

\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
peak value in the sweep.
Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.49$) yields a
4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
threshold choice.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.17 & 1.17 \\
 & TTR & 0.88 & 0.88 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.76 & 0.76 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.55 & 0.55 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & tail decay & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.76$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.08$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.55$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
\label{tab:holdout-split}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\
 & TTR & 0.61 & 0.59 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.59 & 0.01 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.62 & 0.60 & 0.02 & 0.62 & 0.61 & 0.01 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.39 & 0.36 & 0.03 & 0.38 & 0.37 & 0.01 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.05 & 0.05 & 0.00 & 0.04 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\
 & tail decay & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.02 & 0.11 & 0.07 & 0.04 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.

Selection and validation subsets produce identical partitions in both splits (Table~\ref{tab:holdout-split}; Figure~\ref{fig:holdout-scatter}).
The maximum $\Delta|\rho|$ between selection and validation is 0.05 (entropy std, Split~B), and the minimum gap between adjacent zones remains $>$0.15 in all subsets.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_ddr_holdout_split.pdf}
\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

Levene tests reject equal variance between gen-1 and gen-2+ for drifting features ($p < 10^{-10}$; variance ratios 1.86--2.21).
To verify that the DDR partition is robust to this heteroscedasticity, we supplement pooled Cohen's $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ (using the gen-1 standard deviation as denominator) and Cliff's $\delta$ (a non-parametric ordinal effect size; Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
\label{tab:effect-sizes}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & ent.\ mean & 1.054 & 1.410 & 0.587 \\
 & TTR & 0.814 & 1.116 & 0.510 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.735 & 0.936 & 0.528 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & ent.\ std & 0.457 & 0.605 & 0.295 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & tail decay & 0.087 & 0.099 & 0.072 \\
 & ent.\ max & 0.062 & 0.065 & 0.021 \\
 & ent.\ min & 0.016 & 0.015 & 0.354$^{\dagger}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\noindent Effect sizes in Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes} are computed on the binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); the main text (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reports 3-class pooled $d$ values (e.g., hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), which are slightly larger because the gen-0/gen-1 contrast contributes additional separation.
Glass's $\Delta$ amplifies drifting effects (1.41 vs.\ 1.05 for entropy mean) because gen-2+ variance exceeds gen-1 variance (ratio 2.08), making the pooled Cohen's $d$ conservative.
Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.
Cliff's $\delta$ classifies all drifting features as ``large'' ($|\delta| > 0.474$) and entropy std as ``small'' ($|\delta|{=}0.295$), consistent with the parametric partition.

\noindent $^{\dagger}$Entropy min's elevated Cliff's $\delta$ (0.354, ``medium'') reflects distributional shape asymmetry between gen-1 and gen-2+ that rank-based statistics detect but location measures do not (Cohen's $d{=}0.016$, Glass's $\Delta{=}0.015$).
This is consistent with its documented boundary status (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}): the gen-0/gen-1 transition produces rank-order shifts that persist into deeper generations without affecting the mean.
